summary: This informational document presents a high-level architecture for building data-center network virtualization over Layer 3. It describes the major components of such a system and aims to divide the problem into smaller pieces that can be implemented separately.

plainLanguage.summary: In a big data center, many customers share the same wires but each should see their own private network. This draws the big picture of how to do that.

questions: what is a network virtualization edge
difference between l2 and l3 virtual networks
subtitle: Blueprint for building virtual networks on top of the data-center IP fabric.

tldr.problem: Data centers host many independent tenants, each requiring isolated networks. Running separate physical networks per tenant is expensive and inflexible.
tldr.mechanism: NVO3 uses overlay tunnels to decouple virtual networks from the physical data-center IP infrastructure. Network Virtualization Edges (NVEs) encapsulate tenant traffic and tunnel it across the IP network, while a Network Virtualization Authority (NVA) manages address mappings.
tldr.outcome: Tenants get isolated L2 or L3 virtual networks independent of physical topology, enabling multi-tenancy, VM mobility, and flexible network policies without requiring physical network changes.

today: RFC 8014 is Informational and provides the foundational architecture that multiple standardized encapsulation formats (VXLAN, NVGRE, Geneve) and control protocols (EVPN, OVSDB) have been built upon. Many data centers now use NVO3 architectures in production, particularly in cloud environments.

sections.title: The Challenge of Multi-Tenant Data Centers
sections.content:
Data centers consolidate many independent tenants on shared infrastructure. Each tenant expects a private network with its own IP addresses, broadcast domains, and security policies, as if they had their own dedicated network.

Traditional approaches—one physical network per tenant—are expensive and inflexible. When a virtual machine (VM) moves from one server to another, its network settings must follow. When a tenant grows or shrinks, physical rewiring becomes necessary.

Network Virtualization over Layer 3 (NVO3) solves this by decoupling virtual networks from the physical IP infrastructure. Instead of creating separate physical networks, NVO3 tunnels tenant traffic across the underlying IP network. The physical data-center network becomes a simple best-effort delivery service; tenants see isolated virtual networks above it.

This architecture document describes the major components of an NVO3 system and how they interact. It is not a standards document but rather a framework for thinking about the problem space, allowing implementers to build and deploy components independently.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of giving each customer their own set of wires, you wrap each customer's traffic in a tunnel and run all the tunnels across the same shared wires. The shared network does not need to understand what is inside the tunnels.

sections.title: The NVO3 Components
sections.content:
An NVO3 system has three major architectural components.

Network Virtualization Edge (NVE): The NVE is the boundary point where tenant traffic enters and exits the overlay network. It encapsulates outgoing tenant traffic in a tunnel header and decapsulates arriving tunneled traffic. An NVE can be implemented on a hypervisor with VMs, on a physical switch port facing a bare-metal server, or on a standalone gateway appliance. The NVE maintains local state about each virtual network it serves: which remote NVEs host other tenants on the same VN, how to reach them, and what context identifier (VNI—Virtual Network Identifier) to use in the tunnel header.

Network Virtualization Authority (NVA): The NVA is the control plane that holds the master mapping of addresses to locations. It knows which tenant addresses (MAC and IP) are attached to which NVEs and distributes that information to NVEs. When an NVE needs to send traffic to a remote tenant, it queries the NVA to learn the remote NVE's address. The NVA can be centralized or distributed; what matters is that NVEs see it as a single, consistent service.

Virtual Network (VN): A VN is a logical network offering either L2 (Ethernet-like) or L3 (IP-like) service to tenants. Tenant Systems connected to the same VN can communicate with each other; communication with other VNs is blocked by policy unless explicitly allowed.

These three components interact: NVEs use the NVA to learn how to reach remote tenants, then encapsulate and tunnel traffic across the IP underlay.
sections.plainLanguage: The NVE is the boundary where customer packets enter the tunnel system. The NVA is the directory that says 'that customer is over there on that NVE.' Tunnel that traffic across the shared network to the right NVE, and the NVE on the far end unwraps it.

sections.title: Service Models and Tenant Connectivity
sections.content:
NVO3 supports both L2 and L3 virtual networks, each with different characteristics.

L2 Service (Ethernet emulation): The NVE transports Ethernet frames between tenants on the same VN based on MAC addresses. To a tenant, the VN appears like a private VLAN. Broadcast and multicast frames are delivered to all tenant members (or relevant multicast group members) on the VN. The NVE must forward frames based on MAC learning or query the NVA for MAC-to-NVE mappings. This service is useful for legacy systems or protocols that expect native Ethernet access.

L3 Service (IP routing): The NVE routes IP packets between tenants, ignoring MAC addresses. Tenants are configured with point-to-point IP subnets (essentially one tenant and one gateway per subnet). The NVE forwards packets based on IP destination addresses. This service is simpler and scales better than L2 because it reduces broadcast domain size and avoids MAC learning overhead.

Combined L2/L3 Service: Some deployments offer both simultaneously: L2 service within a VN for tenant-to-tenant communication, and L3 service for traffic entering or leaving the VN (e.g., through a gateway router).

Tenants connect to an NVE via a Virtual Access Point (VAP), which is a logical port on the NVE associated with a specific VN. A single NVE can support many VAPs for different VNs. Tenant Systems can be VMs on a hypervisor, bare-metal servers connected to a switch port, or network service appliances like firewalls or load balancers.
sections.plainLanguage: L2 service is like each customer has their own Ethernet switch. L3 service is like each customer has their own router. The NVE can act as either (or both), depending on what the customer needs.

sections.title: Address Dissemination and State Management
sections.content:
For an NVE to tunnel traffic to a remote tenant, it must know where that tenant's address is located—i.e., which NVE currently hosts it. The address dissemination process builds and maintains this mapping information.

There are two primary approaches. First, learning: NVEs learn tenant addresses by observing incoming traffic, similar to how L2 bridges learn MAC addresses. When tenant X sends a frame from NVE-A, NVE-A learns 'tenant X is here.' But learning alone is inefficient, especially in large deployments, because the first packet to a destination must be flooded, and the NVE never learns addresses from traffic it does not see locally.

Second, address distribution: The NVA maintains a database of all tenant addresses and their locations. When an NVE attaches a new tenant, it notifies the NVA. When another NVE needs to reach that tenant, it queries the NVA instead of relying on learning. This eliminates flooding and ensures scalability.

Each NVE maintains several types of local state: (1) which tenants are attached to which VAPs, (2) mappings from tenant addresses to remote NVEs, (3) for multicast traffic, which remote NVEs participate in which groups, (4) the encapsulation type and VNI to use, and (5) any per-VN policies such as QoS or ACLs.

NVEs can be multihomed—connected to the underlay through multiple interfaces or paths. In such cases, the address mapping must handle one-to-many relationships (one tenant reachable through multiple NVE addresses) and enable failover if one path becomes unavailable.
sections.plainLanguage: The NVA is like a telephone directory: NVEs ask 'where is tenant X?' and the NVA answers 'they are on NVE-B.' Each NVE keeps a local copy of the parts of the directory it needs.

sections.title: Gateway Functions and Inter-VN Communication
sections.content:
While most communication in NVO3 is within a single VN (tenant to tenant on the same network), gateways enable communication across VN boundaries and to external networks.

Gateway types: Gateways can be L2 bridges or L3 routers, and they can be centralized (a single point of control) or distributed (implemented on each NVE).

  • L2 gateways bridge between VNs or legacy L2 networks. They forward based on MAC addresses and allow L2 broadcast to propagate.
  • L3 gateways route between VNs or external IP networks. They understand IP addresses and apply routing policies.
  • Distributed gateways implement gateway functions directly on NVEs. Instead of routing all inter-VN traffic through a central device, each NVE can make local forwarding decisions if it has access to the policy information from the NVA. This avoids triangular routing and hair-pinning.

Whether inter-VN communication is allowed is a matter of policy. By default, different VNs are isolated. The NVA maintains policy information about which VNs can communicate, and NVEs enforce this locally if they implement distributed gateway functions.

Gateways also handle special cases: bare-metal servers without NVE functionality can connect via a gateway, legacy VLAN networks can bridge to overlay VNs, and external connectivity (Internet or VPN) flows through gateways.
sections.plainLanguage: Gateways are doors between customer networks. A central gateway is one door that all cross-network traffic goes through. Distributed gateways mean each NVE has permission to route between networks directly, avoiding bottlenecks.

sections.title: Control Protocols and Deployment
sections.content:
NVE-NVA Control Protocol: NVEs and NVAs must communicate to exchange address mappings and network state. The protocol has bidirectional information flow. NVE-to-NVA: when a tenant attaches to an NVE, the NVE notifies the NVA 'tenant X is on my VAP Y.' When a tenant detaches, the NVE sends notification. NVEs also report errors when reaching remote tenants. NVA-to-NVE: when an NVE needs to reach a remote tenant, it queries the NVA and gets the NVE address(es) hosting it. Rather than pushing all mappings to all NVEs, NVEs subscribe to updates for only the VNs they serve, improving scalability. The NVA can be implemented in multiple ways: a centralized database with APIs, a distributed system using routing protocols like BGP, or a replicated cluster. In environments with VM orchestration (VMware, OpenStack), the NVA can obtain information directly from the orchestration system.

Deployment Scenarios: The NVO3 architecture supports several models. VM-based overlay: NVE functionality runs in the hypervisor or virtual switch on each server; this is common in cloud data centers but uses server CPU. Split-NVE: the NVE is split between hypervisor and a Top-of-Rack switch; the switch handles encapsulation and offloads CPU work. Gateway appliances: security appliances or load balancers act as NVEs; they communicate directly with the NVA. Bare-metal servers: connect via static switch port configuration. These models can coexist—a data center might have VM-based NVEs on most servers, split-NVEs on high-performance servers, gateways for legacy systems, and bare-metal servers on switch ports.
sections.plainLanguage: The control protocol is how NVEs ask the NVA 'where is this customer?' The NVE can run on a hypervisor, a network switch, or a separate appliance—different deployments use what works best for them.

layers.label: Tenant Applications
layers.detail: VMs, containers, bare-metal apps; see isolated virtual networks

layers.label: Overlay Tunnels
layers.detail: Encapsulated tenant packets; traverse underlay network

layers.label: Data-Center IP Network (Underlay)
layers.detail: Standard IP routing; delivers tunnel packets between NVEs

left.title: Centralized Gateway
left.desc: All cross-VN traffic goes through one central device; creates potential bottleneck but simpler policy control.

right.title: Distributed Gateway
right.desc: NVEs route between VNs directly using policy from NVA; avoids bottleneck and enables direct, optimal paths.
